lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Life Cycle of the Housefly

pages.body:
You have probably seen a housefly land on food, buzz around a dustbin, or rest on a wall. But a fly does not start life looking like this. It goes through several very different stages before it becomes the fly you recognise.

> **Did you know?** A single female housefly can lay up to 500 eggs in her lifetime, usually in batches of about 75 to 150 at a time.

- Have you ever seen small white worms wriggling in rubbish or rotten fruit? Those may be young houseflies.

Before looking at how a housefly grows, it helps to know what kind of animal it is. The housefly, scientific name Musca domestica, belongs to a large group of animals called insects.

pages.title: The housefly is an insect
pages.body:
- Its body is divided into three main parts: a head, a thorax and an abdomen.
- It has six legs, all attached to the thorax.
- It has one pair of wings, which is unusual since most insects have two pairs.
- It has large compound eyes made up of thousands of tiny lenses, which give it very wide vision.

[[img:ik87wm5f0]]

The housefly goes through four stages in its life, and each stage looks completely different from the last. This kind of life cycle, where the young and the adult look very different, is called complete metamorphosis.

[[img:idr3pjbg1]]
[[img:ijxhuayu2]]

| **Stage** | **What it looks like and does** |
|---|---|
| Egg | Tiny, white and oval. A female fly lays her eggs in warm, moist places such as rotten food, manure or rubbish. |
| Larva (maggot) | A soft, legless, worm-like creature that hatches from the egg. It feeds constantly and grows quickly. |
| Pupa | The larva stops feeding, its skin hardens into a brown case, and inside this case its body changes completely. |
| Adult | A fully grown fly breaks out of the pupa case. It has wings, six legs, and can fly and reproduce. |

> **DEFINITION** **Life cycle:** the stages a living thing passes through, from the start of its life until it is able to reproduce. **Complete metamorphosis:** a type of life cycle in which the young stages of an organism look completely different from the adult stage.

pages.body:
> **A housefly can complete its whole life cycle, from egg to adult, in as little as seven to ten days in warm weather.**

## How quickly houseflies multiply

A female housefly lays her eggs in batches in warm, moist waste and may lay several hundred eggs in her lifetime. The eggs hatch into maggots within about a day in warm weather. Because the life cycle is so short and each female lays so many eggs, a few flies can become a very large number in a few weeks if waste is not removed.

A fly lands on a pile of rubbish, then a few minutes later lands on your food. Think about where that fly has been and what might be on its legs and body.

- Where do you usually see houseflies in your home or community?
- Why do you think adults often tell you to cover your food?

Houseflies feed on dead animals, rotten food, manure, and solid and liquid waste. Because of this feeding habit, they pick up germs on their legs and body, then carry these germs wherever they land next, including on human food.

This makes the housefly a menace, meaning it causes harm and nuisance to humans, in three main ways.

> **DEFINITION** **Menace:** a person, animal or thing that is likely to cause harm, danger or serious nuisance.

**How houseflies cause harm**
- Spread disease. Germs picked up from waste can be dropped onto food, spreading diseases such as dysentery.
- Cause food poisoning. Eating food that a fly has contaminated can make a person seriously ill.
- Create nuisance. Large numbers of flies are unpleasant, disturb daily activities, and are a sign of poor waste management nearby.

**How to reduce the harm**
- Cover all food and store waste in closed, covered bins.
- Dispose of rubbish, manure and rotten food quickly and properly.
- Keep kitchens, compounds and toilets clean to remove breeding places.
- Use screens on windows and doors, or fly traps, to keep flies away from food.

pages.body:
> **Reducing housefly breeding places is more effective than fighting flies after they appear.**

## How a housefly carries germs

The body and legs of a housefly are covered with fine hairs and its feet have sticky pads. When the fly walks on rubbish, faeces or rotten food, germs stick to these parts. A fly cannot chew solid food. It spits a drop of digestive juice onto the food to soften it and then sucks up the liquid. The vomit and droppings it leaves on food can also carry germs.

The germs carried by houseflies cause several illnesses.

- Dysentery, which causes severe diarrhoea with blood in the stools.
- Cholera, which causes severe watery diarrhoea and loss of body water.
- Typhoid fever, which causes high fever, headache and stomach pain.
- Food poisoning, which causes vomiting and stomach cramps.

Washing the hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet gives extra protection against these illnesses.

parts.a: The body and legs are covered with fine hairs and the feet have sticky pads, so germs from rubbish, faeces or rotten food stick to them. Its vomit and droppings can also carry germs.

ideas.t: Fine hairs on the body and legs

ideas.t: It spits digestive juice to soften the food

questions.q: Name two diseases spread by houseflies apart from dysentery.

parts.a: Cholera and typhoid fever.

pages.body:
- The housefly goes through four stages of complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa and adult.
- Each stage looks completely different from the one before it.
- A housefly can complete its whole life cycle in as little as seven to ten days in warm weather.
- Houseflies feed on dead animals, rotten food, manure and waste, which allows them to pick up and spread germs.
- Houseflies can spread disease, cause food poisoning, and create nuisance in the environment.
- Covering food, managing waste properly, and keeping surroundings clean are effective ways to reduce housefly problems.
- A female housefly lays several hundred eggs, so houseflies multiply very fast where waste is left uncovered.
- Houseflies carry germs on their hairy legs, sticky feet, vomit and droppings, and can spread dysentery, cholera and typhoid fever.

| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Life cycle | The stages a living thing passes through from the start of its life to when it can reproduce |
| Complete metamorphosis | A life cycle in which the young stages look completely different from the adult |
| Insect | An animal with a body divided into a head, a thorax and an abdomen, six legs, and usually wings |
| Compound eye | An eye made up of many tiny lenses, giving very wide vision |
| Larva | The worm-like young stage of an insect that hatches from an egg |
| Pupa | The resting stage during which a larva's body changes into an adult |
| Menace | Something that causes harm, danger or serious nuisance |
| Dysentery | A disease that causes severe diarrhoea, which can be spread by houseflies |
| Contaminate | To make something dirty or unsafe by adding germs or harmful substances |
| Breeding place | A location where an organism lays eggs and its young develop |
